entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Sykes–Picot Agreement, formalized on May 16, 1916, was a clandestine diplomatic arrangement between the United Kingdom and France, with the assent of Tsarist Russia, aimed at delineating spheres of influence and control in the Middle East following the anticipated defeat of the Ottoman Empire in World War I. This agreement, named after the British diplomat Mark Sykes and French diplomat François Georges-Picot, set the stage for the modern political landscape of the Middle East, impacting millions and fueling regional tensions that persist to this day. The agreement's significance lies in its role in the arbitrary division of territories, disregarding ethnic and sectarian borders, which has had lasting ramifications for national identity and conflict in the region.

The agreement proposed that the French would gain control over southeastern Turkey, northern Iraq, Syria, and Lebanon, while the British would oversee southern Iraq, Jordan, and Palestine, marked by a series of lines drawn on a map that ignored the realities of the local populations. The Sykes-Picot arrangements were part of a broader strategy by the Allied powers to secure their interests in the region, as evidenced by the Balfour Declaration later in 1917, which promised a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine, further complicating the geopolitical landscape. This clandestine deal was only partially realized post-war, as the League of Nations mandates redefined the borders, but the core ideas of Western imperial influence remained entrenched in the new geopolitical order.
